constructions.title: Multi-force work–energy ledger
core1a: Choose the moving object/system and direction of displacement
Identify all forces including gravity, friction and normal
Calculate signed work per force and sum to net work
Use W_net=ΔK, not W_friction=ΔK
Check geometry, omitted forces and no-motion boundary
core1b: Predict sign of change in kinetic energy from competing forces
Construct a full force-work ledger without suggested formula order
Reconstruct the velocity using total work rather than one force
Diagnose an omitted-gravity or wrong-friction-sign solution
Repair by explicitly restoring missing ledger row
Boundary test: change the incline height or remove the motor
constructions.misconception: Using one selected force's work as net work or treating friction as always the only energy loss

constructions.title: Spring contact and motion phases
core1a: Draw the compressed-spring contact region and natural-length release boundary
Calculate spring energy ½kx² while in contact
Determine the energy and speed precisely when contact ends
Use a different energy/work equation beyond contact
Explain why spring force is zero after separation when spring is not attached
core1b: Predict when the spring stops pushing
Split a new motion into contact and post-contact phases
Reconstruct the energy ledger for each phase
Diagnose a solution that keeps spring force active after separation
Repair the region boundary before recalculating
Boundary test: change the surface friction only after separation
constructions.misconception: Continuing to apply the spring force and spring work outside the actual contact region

constructions.title: Constant power and speed–time–distance
core1a: Distinguish constant power from constant force
Start with P=dK/dt and show K increases linearly with t if P constant and losses negligible
From ½mv²=Pt for rest-start derive v∝√t
Relate distance to area under a v–t curve; reserve s∝t^(3/2) for a supported algebra/calculus extension
Check start-speed and resistive-loss conditions
core1b: Choose constant-P rather than constant-F model
Predict qualitative v–t shape and KE–t straight line
Reconstruct speed at two times from energy inputs
Diagnose unjustified constant acceleration
Repair model and test a nonzero-start-speed case
Boundary test: add friction or efficiency loss
constructions.misconception: Treating constant motor power as constant force or constant acceleration

constructions.title: Distributed mass, chain and changing centre of mass
core1a: Represent a hanging length and its fraction of the chain mass
Find the hanging segment's centre-of-mass height
Build changing potential energy as hanging length changes
Compare finite-state energy method with integral where curriculum supports it
Check limits: none hanging vs all hanging
core1b: Represent a new hanging-rope geometry without a memorized cable formula
Identify which mass is lifted and its moving centre of mass
Reconstruct the needed work from potential energy
Diagnose using total chain mass at full height
Repair hanging-fraction calculation
Boundary test: different fraction or rope length
constructions.misconception: Treating every part of a partly hanging chain as being raised through the same height

constructions.title: Graph decision: area, slope or time shape
core1a: Read both axes and their units before computing
Force–displacement graph: signed area is work
Potential–position graph: negative slope is conservative force
Displacement–time graph: slope is velocity, not work
Check whether the source's original graph/axes are actually available
core1b: Select the correct operation from a newly authored graph with changed axes
Compute a signed area, negative slope or velocity as appropriate
Explain why the other two operations are wrong for those units
Diagnose area–slope confusion
Repair by labeling axes and dimensional check
Boundary test: switch to a different graph type
constructions.misconception: Applying 'area under graph' indiscriminately even when the axes are not force and displacement

constructions.title: Vertical circle: energy plus contact/tension condition
core1a: Use height to convert energy into speed at each location
Distinguish radial acceleration v²/r from tangential acceleration
Balance inward forces at top/bottom of a circular path
Apply T≥0 for a string or N≥0 for a contact constraint
Check when computed negative tension means loss of taut-string model
core1b: Model both height/speed and radial contact force
Choose actual radial direction at a new location
Reconstruct minimum-speed condition rather than recall a shortcut
Diagnose a negative-tension answer being treated as physical
Repair with contact-loss interpretation
Boundary test: different top speed or track radius
constructions.misconception: Energy conservation alone guaranteeing the object stays in a vertical circle

constructions.title: Variable-mass momentum transfer and conveyor power
core1a: Identify incoming mass per unit time and velocity change
Explain why momentum per unit time sets force
Distinguish motor work/power from purely kinetic-energy flow
Account for losses or impact behavior only when specified
core1b: Predict the direction and size of the push needed when material joins a moving belt
Attempt: draw incoming and outgoing horizontal momenta per unit time and choose the correct control volume
Reconstruct momentum-transfer force and supplied motor power, explaining each energy flow
Diagnose treating the whole accumulated load as one fixed-mass body
Repair the control-volume boundaries and restore missing momentum-flow terms
Boundary test: change incoming feed direction or belt speed
constructions.misconception: Confusing momentum flow with total momentum of a fixed body

constructions.title: Spring energy at equal force versus equal extension
core1a: State stored energy U=½kx² and spring force magnitude F=kx
Hold extension fixed: U grows with k
Hold force fixed: substitute x=F/k, giving U=F²/(2k)
Use a controlled-variable comparison before selecting a formula
core1b: Predict whether the stiffer spring stores more energy when the force is fixed versus when extension is fixed
Attempt: identify the controlled variable in two new experiments and write separate energy models
Reconstruct which spring stores more energy in each experiment using the appropriate equations
Diagnose assuming higher stiffness always means greater stored energy
Repair by explicitly marking the held-fixed variable in each comparison
Boundary test: double stiffness in each protocol and compare the two changes
constructions.misconception: Ignoring which variable is controlled when comparing springs

learner_protocol: Ask for an explanation and a model/diagram before exposing author solutions; hints optional after committed attempt. Post-attempt rubric separates model choice, sign/conditions, working, and changed-boundary response. A text-length threshold is not a reasoning assessment.

WPE-C03.unit_rule: W=J/s, no resistance and positive initial speed

WPE-C05.unit_rule: F-x area work, U-x negative slope force, s-t slope velocity, F-t area impulse

WPE-C06.unit_rule: For taut string top: mg+T=mv^2/r, T>=0; height gain top-bottom=2r

WPE-C07.unit_rule: Steady conveyor pickup at constant belt speed; rate in kg/s, F=rate*(v-u), motor pickup power=F*v, chips' K gain rate=rate*(v²-u²)/2, sliding heat=rate*(v-u)²/2; u<v, no other losses.

WPE-C08.unit_rule: Quasistatic elastic Hookean spring: F_final=k*x, U=k*x²/2=F_final²/(2k). Fixed extension and fixed final force are different comparisons.
